To establish a fair day’s work, the task must first be broken into its elementary motions, and each motion timed with a stopwatch under ordinary conditions. Allowances are then added for rest, unavoidable delays, and the fatigue that accumulates through the day. The resulting standard time is not an average of what workers happen to do; it is an estimate of what a trained worker can accomplish at a sustained pace without injury. Critics object that this approach treats the worker as a machine, and in some implementations it has. But the underlying principle, that methods should be studied and compared by measurement rather than left to tradition, applies equally well to improving tools, layouts, and training, and these improvements benefit workers as much as employers.
